turns.prompt_text: I'm using general electric silicone type 2 to try to adhese two panes of glass together, I pressed it on 12 hours ago and it is still not dry
turns.response_html:
It can be frustrating when a project stays tacky longer than expected, especially with glass where you want that immediate clarity and bond. GE Silicone 2 is a neutral-cure sealant, which behaves differently than the more common "vinegar-smelling" acetoxy-cure silicones.

Here is why your glass panes might still be wet and what you can do about it:

1. The "Sandwich" Effect (Lack of Air)

Silicone 2 requires exposure to atmospheric moisture to cure. When you press two non-porous surfaces like glass together, you create an airtight seal.

  • The Problem: Only the very edges of the silicone are exposed to the air. The "inner" silicone is essentially trapped and cannot react with moisture to harden.
  • The Fix: If the bond is critical and the surface area is large, you may need to apply the silicone in beads or "dots" to allow air paths, or simply wait much longer—potentially several days—for the cure to work its way inward from the perimeter.

2. Temperature and Humidity

Neutral-cure silicones are sensitive to their environment.

  • Cold Air: If your workspace is below 10°C (50°F), the chemical reaction slows down significantly.
  • Dry Air: Because it needs moisture to cure, extremely low humidity can stall the process.
  • The Fix: Gently increasing the humidity in the room (using a humidifier or even a bowl of warm water nearby) and ensuring the temperature is at least 20°C (68°F) can help jumpstart the process.

3. Application Thickness

If you applied a very thick layer to fill a gap, it will take much longer than the standard "tack-free" time listed on the tube. Most ratings are based on a thin bead; a thick "sandwich" layer can take 48 to 72 hours to reach full strength even under ideal conditions.

4. Product Age (The "Expired" Factor)

Silicone has a shelf life. If the tube is several years old or has been stored in extreme heat, the curing agents can break down.

  • The Test: Squeeze a small amount onto a piece of cardboard. If it hasn't formed a "skin" within an hour, the tube is likely expired and will never fully cure.

Next Steps:

  • Don't Move It: Since it's still wet, moving the glass now could create bubbles or streaks that will be visible once it finally dries.
  • Airflow: Point a small fan toward the glass. While it needs moisture, moving air helps carry away the byproducts of the curing reaction (methanol in the case of Type 2).

If it's still completely liquid after 24 hours, you likely have an airflow or expiration issue and may need to separate the panes, clean them with mineral spirits, and try a different application method.

turns.prompt_text: What can I do with expired silicone type 2?
turns.response_html:
It is a bit of a letdown when a tool in the kit fails right when you need it. Unfortunately, once silicone has "expired" and lost its ability to cure, it loses almost all of its structural and sealing utility. Because the chemical cross-linking agents have broken down, it will likely remain a sticky, goopy mess forever rather than turning into rubber.

Since you can't use it for its intended purpose, here is how to handle it:

1. The "Grip" Hack (Non-Critical Use)

If the silicone is still somewhat capable of thickening (even if it won't fully harden), you can use it for low-stakes, non-permanent grip:

  • Tool Handles: Smear a thin layer on the handles of a wrench or hammer and wrap it in electrical tape. The silicone acts as a vibration-dampening filler inside the tape.
  • Rug Backing: If you are working on a rug or mat, small dabs on the underside can sometimes provide enough "tack" to keep it from sliding on a hard floor, though it may leave a residue.

2. Practice and Prototyping

If you are teaching someone how to lay a bead or working on a complex joint design:

  • Caulking Practice: Use the expired tube to practice your "pulling" technique on scrap wood or cardboard. It’s better to mess up with the "trash" tube than the expensive new one.
  • Volume Testing: If you need to know exactly how much volume a gap requires before opening a fresh tube, use the expired stuff to fill the space and measure the displacement.

3. Proper Disposal (Important)

Since expired silicone won't cure, it remains a chemical mess that can easily ruin clothes, workbenches, and flooring.

  • Do Not Flush: Never wash it down a drain; it will stick to pipes and cause massive clogs.
  • Solidify it: Squeeze the remaining contents onto a piece of scrap cardboard or into a disposable plastic tub. Mix it with some sawdust, dirt, or cat litter to soak up the oils and turn it into a solid "puck."
  • Trash: Once it’s contained and mixed with an absorbent, it can typically go into your regular household trash (check your local Ames/Story County guidelines for hazardous waste if you have a large bulk quantity).

4. Salvage the Tube

If you have a reusable caulking gun, make sure to clean the plunger and tip immediately. Expired silicone is notoriously difficult to clean once it migrates into the moving parts of your tools. Use mineral spirits or isopropyl alcohol to wipe down any metal surfaces it touched.

A quick tip for the future: To keep your next tube fresh longer, squeeze a small bit out of the nozzle and leave it there to cure into a "plug," or use a dedicated silicone cap. Storing it in a cool, dry place (not a humid garage) can also help stretch that expiration date.
